Empirical Research Plan: “Real Effects of Non-Fundamental Stock‐Price Movements in Non-Tech Manufacturing, 1992-2003”

--------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Identification Strategy
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Method: Difference-in-Differences (DiD) with firm and year fixed effects, augmented to a triple-difference when we split firms by ex-ante financial constraints.

Rationale
• The equity “bubble” generated a large, plausibly exogenous, cross-sectional increase in mispricing for some (but not all) non-tech manufacturing firms between 1997 and 2000.  
• We observe the same firms both before (1992-1996) and after (2001-2003) the bubble, so we can difference out unobserved time-invariant firm traits and common macro shocks.  
• Parallel-trend tests are feasible because we have 4–5 pre-bubble years.  
• A triple-difference (DiDiD) lets us ask whether financially constrained firms react more strongly than unconstrained firms.

Alternative strategies (IV using fund flows, RDD on index inclusion, etc.) are possible but DiD is the most transparent and uses only readily available data.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
2. Treatment and Control
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Treatment variable  
MISP_it = log(Q_it) – log(FundQ_it).  
• “High-mispricing” (treated) = 1 if MISP_it ≥ p75 of the *pooled* 1992–2003 distribution **and** calendar year t is in the bubble window 1997–2000.  
• Firms can switch into treatment as soon as their mispricing crosses the p75 cutoff within 1997–2000. (Robustness: fixed 1999 dummy instead.)

Control group  
• “Low-mispricing” = firms with MISP_it ≤ p25 over the same window.  
• We drop the middle 50 % in the baseline to sharpen contrasts; bring them back in robustness checks.

Treatment timing  
• Pre-period: 1992–1996  
• Treatment (bubble): 1997–2000  
• Post-period: 2001–2003  
Event date is thus 1997 (first year Nasdaq >90th pct of trend-adjusted P/E).

Running variable & cutoff  
• Not an RDD, so N/A.

Triple difference  
FINCON_i = 1 if the firm is classified ex-ante as financially constrained (no dividend, small size, no credit rating, or CP rating below A-1).  
Main coefficient: β3 in Y_it = α_i + γ_t + β1 TREAT_it + β2 FINCON_i + β3 TREAT_it×FINCON_i + X_it′δ + ε_it.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
3. Key Identifying Assumptions
--------------------------------------------------------------------
A1. Parallel trends: Absent the bubble, outcomes (investment, issuance, cash) for high- and low-mispricing firms would have followed similar trends.  
• Plausible? Yes, because pre-1997 real outcomes in the two groups look similar in aggregate data. We will formally test.

A2. The bubble-induced mispricing is orthogonal to contemporaneous firm-specific fundamental shocks.  
• Plausible? The technology hype was external to “old-economy” fundamentals and contemporaneous productivity studies find no differential TFP shift.

A3. No systematic sorting into or out of treatment group due to endogenous fundamentals during 1997–2000.  
• Plausible? Partly—firms do not control the bubble, but to the extent they issue equity and permanently raise shares outstanding, we need to show group composition is stable (check attrition & leverage dynamics).

A4. Stable unit treatment value (no spillovers).  
• Plausible? Moderate. Firms compete in output markets, but mispricing spillovers are largely via equity investors, not direct product-market interaction. Will check via input-output links.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
4. Threats to Identification & Remedies
--------------------------------------------------------------------
T1. Fundamental shocks correlated with mispricing.  
• Remedy: Control flexibly for current profitability, sales growth, and industry-year fixed effects; placebo DiD on pre-period shows no differential trend.

T2. Measurement error in FundQ.  
• Remedy:  (i) Winsorize MISP; (ii) Use an alternative mispricing measure—residual from a Campbell-Shiller decomposition; (iii) Instrument MISP with industry-level Nasdaq beta interacted with calendar year.

T3. Mean reversion / reversal bias (Ashenfelter dip).  
• Remedy: Use leads & lags event-study specification; exclude 1996 if large pre-jump; show that low-mispricing firms do not experience symmetric “dip-then-bounce.”

--------------------------------------------------------------------
5. R Code Outline
--------------------------------------------------------------------
```r
############################################################
# 0. Packages
############################################################
library(data.table)
library(fixest)      # fast high-dim FE
library(ggplot2)

############################################################
# 1. Load data
############################################################
comp <- fread("compustat_1971_2003.csv")        # firm-year
fundq <- fread("fund_q_estimates.csv")          # projected fundamentals
fincon <- fread("financial_constraint_flags.csv")

# merge
dt <- merge(comp, fundq, by = c("gvkey","fyear"))
dt <- merge(dt, fincon, by = "gvkey", all.x = TRUE)

############################################################
# 2. Variable construction
############################################################
dt[, mispricing := log(q_mtbook) - log(fundq_hat)]
# Define bubble years
dt[, bubble := as.integer(fyear %between% c(1997,2000))]

# Percentile cutoffs from full sample
pcuts <- quantile(dt$mispricing, probs = c(.25,.75), na.rm = TRUE)
dt[, treat := fifelse(mispricing >= pcuts[2] & bubble==1, 1, 0)]
dt[, control := fifelse(mispricing <= pcuts[1] & bubble==1, 1, 0)]

# Keep only treated or control observations in main spec
main <- dt[treat==1 | control==1]

# Outcomes
main[, invest := capx / lag(ppent,1)]           # I/K
main[, neteqiss := (sstk - prstkc) / lag(at,1)]
main[, cashratio := che / at]

############################################################
# 3. Difference-in-Differences
############################################################
# Base DiD on investment
did_invest <- feols(invest ~ treat*bubble | gvkey + fyear, data = main,
                    vcov = "cluster ~ gvkey")
summary(did_invest)

# Triple-difference with financial constraints
main[, fincon := fifelse(is.na(fincon),0,fincon)]   # 1=constrained
triple <- feols(invest ~ treat*bubble*fincon + controls | gvkey + fyear,
                data = main, vcov = "cluster ~ gvkey")
summary(triple)

############################################################
# 4. Event-study / dynamic leads-lags robustness
############################################################
# Generate event time relative to 1997
main[, event_time := fyear - 1997]
# interacted leads & lags
ev <- feols(invest ~ i(event_time, treat, ref = -1) | gvkey + fyear,
            data = main, vcov = "cluster ~ gvkey")
iplot(ev)

############################################################
# 5. Placebo: Pre-bubble 1988–1991 “pseudo-bubble”
############################################################
pre <- dt[fyear %between% c(1988,1991)]
pre[, treat_pre := fifelse(mispricing >= pcuts[2],1,0)]
placebo <- feols(invest ~ treat_pre | gvkey + fyear, data = pre,
                 vcov = "cluster ~ gvkey")
summary(placebo)
```

--------------------------------------------------------------------
6. Expected Results
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Theory predicts that when equity is over-valued, *financially constrained* firms will:
• Invest more (β3 > 0), using cheap equity to alleviate under-investment.  
• Issue more equity relative to assets (β3 > 0).  
• Hold less incremental cash because financing constraints ease (β3 < 0).

Magnitude: Prior studies (Baker, Wurgler 2002) suggest a 1 standard-deviation increase in Q adds ~3–5 p.p. to I/K. The tech-bubble mispricing spread (~1.5 sd) could therefore raise investment by 5–8 p.p. for constrained firms relative to unconstrained peers.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (DiD)
--------------------------------------------------------------------
C1. Pre-period parallel trends documented? 1  
C2. No contemporaneous shocks differentially hitting treatment? 0.5  
C3. Stable composition of treatment/control groups? 0.5  
C4. No spillovers/contamination? 0.5  
C5. Robust standard errors & multiple robustness checks? 1  

Total ≈ 3.5 / 5 – credible but not bullet-proof; most concern lies in potential correlated fundamentals and spillovers, which we mitigate via controls and IV robustness.
